source.title: RWKU: Benchmarking Real-World Knowledge Unlearning for Large Language Models
source.authors: Zhuo-Ran Jin; Pengfei Cao; Chenhao Wang; Zhitao He; Hong-Bang Yuan; Jiachun Li; Yubo Chen; Kang Liu; Jun Zhao

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure text is garbled in the extraction, but the main tables and relevant prose are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests how unlearning methods perform under knowledge probes and adversarial prompts, using its own benchmark and measures rather than reproducing one of the named original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports aggregate fill-in-the-blank, question-answer and adversarial-attack scores, and general-ability scores. Its MIA scores measure membership inference rather than recovery of the target knowledge, so they are not rows for these versions. Attack-type results in Figure 4 are not numerically legible in the supplied text; the paper's explicit statements about those types are reflected in the verdicts. The paper averages its main single-target results over 100 targets.
record.test_reason: RWKU is a new benchmark (200 real celebrities, zero-shot unlearning with synthetic forget corpora) aimed at the same question. It reports residual target knowledge after six unlearning methods on two models, with MMLU utility and nine adversarial prompt types. Its results bear on A (does unlearning remove knowledge while keeping ability?) and E (do prompts elicit it?). It uses no fine-tuning, activation-ablation or quantization recovery attacks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that unlearned models are more susceptible to fill-in-the-blank and adversarial probes than to QA probes, and that the methods seem ineffective against MIAs. They also find efficacy hard to balance with locality and utility, and batch-target unlearning harder and prone to collapse. In-context unlearning, GA and NPO perform relatively well (ICU best on LLaMA3, almost no effect on Phi-3), leaving significant room for improvement.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates six unlearning baselines in a zero-shot-target setting using model-generated synthetic forget corpora and its RWKU probes; it does not reproduce the methods or evaluation recipe of the named original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ by model, method, and fine-tuning approach (full fine-tuning versus LoRA). The authors state that ICU works well on LLaMA3 but has almost no effect on Phi-3. Figure 4 describes differences among attack types, including effective prefix injection, affirmative suffix, multiple-choice, and reverse-query attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: After unlearning, the LOSS membership-inference scores on forget members stay close to those on retain members for almost all synthetic-corpus methods (e.g. LLaMA3 NPO Full 278.9 vs 263.2). The authors say these methods fail under MIA.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearned models retain membership-inference signal on the forgotten data.

record.problems: The paper fixes random seeds and reports no error bars. Main single-target results are averages over 100 targets, which can conceal target-level variation. The supplied Figure 4 attack-type scores are not numerically legible, and the paper does not state a chance-level reference for its ROUGE-L scores.
record.rows_left_out: The tables also report fill-in-the-blank scores, other utility measures, neighbor scores, and MIA results. These were left out to stay within 60 rows and focus on question-answer/adversarial-prompt outcomes and general ability. The MIA measure is not a direct knowledge-recovery measure; the other utility measures are not general-ability scores. See Tables 1-2 and Figure 4.

untested.parts: No chance level is defined for ROUGE-L recall on open-ended answers; near-zero is the only reference.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack on unlearned models.
No activation-direction ablation attack. RepE is used as an unlearning method, not a recovery attack. FB-vs-QA gaps hint at blocked access but are not an internal analysis.
Per-attack-type recovery numbers (Figure 4) are not legible in the supplied text. AA and QA use different probe items, so there is no same-fact before/after-attack comparison.
No new method is claimed robust to the attacks.

missing.what: Fill-in-the-blank (FB) forget scores after unlearning. They show memorized knowledge surviving where QA is suppressed (e.g. LLaMA3 RT Full FB 72.7 vs QA 13.4; ICU FB 26.2 vs QA 1.9). Authors say FB probes still detect the knowledge.
missing.locator: Table 1 and Table 2, Forget FB column; Section 5 Overall Results (1)

missing.what: Per-attack-type elicitation (prefix injection, affirmative suffix, multiple choice, reverse query named most effective).

Phi-3 MMLU for ICU (63.9), GA* Full/LoRA (64.4), GA LoRA (64.2), DPO LoRA (64.3), NPO Full (64.2) and RT Full (64.1); also other utility losses (RepE factuality 17.9, DPO factuality 25.8, RT fluency 588.1).
Batch-target unlearning: DPO/NPO fail to unlearn and GA collapses from 30 targets.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1/V5 labels were remapped to A/E. QA-only rows are linked to A only, since plain questions are not a recovery attack. E states for AA rows compare AA with QA recall after the same method, scaled by each model's baseline. This comparison is indirect because AA and QA are different probe items. On Phi-3, AA probes are easier at baseline (55.8 vs 47.4). Several Phi-3 LoRA/RT runs barely unlearned, so recovery cannot be assessed for them. Results average 100 targets with no error bars.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not state a chance-level reference for ROUGE-L recall, so whether targeted scores reach near chance cannot be determined directly from that comparison. It does test general ability and adversarial-prompt outcomes.
No attack fine-tunes an unlearned model on a small unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact set to test recovery.
No activation direction is ablated to test recovery, and the paper does not test whether a method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested.
The study tests its specified adversarial-prompt probes; it does not test arbitrary rephrasings, jailbreaks, languages, or in-context information beyond its probe sets.
No method is tested for resistance to the full set of attacks in the claim.
